title: Running in NYC at Lincoln Center through August 30th (Kerry Washingto...
transcript: It's a stacked cast of five incredibly talented actors, including Kerry Washington and Tony winners, Kara Young and Kecia Lewis In a reimagined version of Whoopi Goldberg's solo show retitled The Whoopi Monologues, each actor gets an extended segment of the show where they inhabit a fictional character, from a self described “junkie” on a reflective trip to Europe to a Jamaican woman describing her bizarre but hilarious relationship to her old white employer. I have to say, I was worried that this material wouldn't work in this format because Whoopi wrote it specifically for herself to perform. But I was very pleasantly surprised. And actually the fact that it worked so well even without her is in itself kind of a statement about her legacy, reminding us of her talent as a writer, not just a performer as she's more widely known. Each segment has a clever premise, it has something to say and often takes us on some surprising twists and turns. And despite sometimes going to some very dark places, Whoopi also imbued it with some of the characteristics of stand up comedy observational humour with clever punch lines. Plus with the help of Whitney White's direction and intimate conversational relationship with the audience. In that way the show kind of manages to have its cake and eat it too. I did like some sections more than others. I think my two favorites were the ones I alluded to earlier, performed by Kara Young and Danielle Pinnock. Kerry Washington, who's also a producer of the show, is actually only performing in the first half of the run, but she's gonna be replaced by Jurnee Smollett, and I actually think Smollett is gonna be a better fit for this role than Kerry Washington is. Dominique Fishback, who some of you might know from the Deuce or Judas and the Black Messiah, was actually out of the performance that I attended, but hers is also by far the shortest section of the show. Meanwhile, Kecia Lewis has, I think, the longest section of the show right at the end, giving a deeply-felt and charismatic performance reflecting on menopause. And like, I didn't necessarily find this section to be as narratively compelling as the others, But it has maybe the most refreshing insight and commentary. And regardless, it all added up to a warm, engaging and thought provoking evening of theatre.
reasoning: Reviewer was pleasantly surprised, praises writing, direction, and performances, with only minor caveats about certain sections being less compelling. Concludes with clear positive recommendation as 'warm, engaging and thought provoking.'
